summary: Describes the IPv6 Jumbo Payload option, which allows packets larger than the normal limit, and the changes TCP and UDP need to use it. It replaced RFC 2147.

plainLanguage.summary: An IPv6 packet carries a 16-bit field for the size of its data, so a normal packet holds at most 65,535 bytes. This RFC adds an option that carries a 32-bit size instead, so a packet can hold up to 4,294,967,295 bytes of data. It only matters on links whose maximum packet size is above 65,575 bytes.

subtitle: How IPv6 packets carry more than 65,535 bytes of data, and what TCP and UDP change to send them.

tldr.problem: The IPv6 header has a 16-bit Payload Length field, so a normal packet can carry at most 65,535 octets of payload. Links with a larger maximum packet size could carry more, and UDP and TCP also have 16-bit limits.
tldr.mechanism: A Hop-by-Hop option called Jumbo Payload carries a 32-bit length, allowing payloads from 65,536 to 4,294,967,295 octets. The IPv6 Payload Length is set to zero, and UDP and TCP get small changes to cope with the larger sizes.
tldr.outcome: Only nodes that can attach to links with an MTU above 65,575 octets need to implement it. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2147 and reports no new known security concerns.

facts.label: IPv6 Payload Length in a jumbogram

today: RFC 2675 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1999. It obsoletes RFC 2147, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Jumbograms Exist
sections.content:
The IPv6 header (RFC 2460) has a 16-bit Payload Length field and therefore supports payloads up to 65,535 octets long. This document specifies an IPv6 hop-by-hop option, the Jumbo Payload option, that carries a 32-bit length field, allowing transmission of IPv6 packets with payloads between 65,536 and 4,294,967,295 octets. Packets with such long payloads are called jumbograms.

The option is relevant only for IPv6 nodes that may be attached to links with a link MTU greater than 65,575 octets, which is 65,535 plus the 40 octets of the IPv6 header. It need not be implemented or understood by IPv6 nodes that do not support attachment to links with such large MTUs. On links with configurable MTUs, the MTU must not be configured above 65,575 octets if there are nodes attached to that link that do not support the option and it cannot be guaranteed that the option will not be sent to them.

The UDP header (RFC 768) has a 16-bit Length field which prevents it from making use of jumbograms. The TCP header (RFC 793) has no Length field, but both the TCP MSS option and the TCP Urgent field are constrained to 16 bits. This document specifies simple enhancements to TCP and UDP to enable them to make use of jumbograms, and an implementation of TCP or UDP on an IPv6 node that supports the Jumbo Payload option must include those enhancements.

The RFC also notes that the 16-bit checksum used by UDP and TCP becomes less accurate as the length of the data being checksummed increases, and that application designers may want to take this into consideration.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6 packet carries a 16-bit field for the size of its data, so a normal packet holds at most 65,535 bytes. This RFC adds an option that carries a 32-bit size instead, so a packet can hold up to 4,294,967,295 bytes of data. It only matters on links whose maximum packet size is above 65,575 bytes.

sections.title: Where the Document Came From
sections.content:
Section 1.1 of the RFC records that the document merges and updates material that was previously published in two separate documents.

The specification of the Jumbo Payload option previously appeared as part of the IPv6 specification in RFC 1883. RFC 1883 has been superseded by RFC 2460, which no longer includes the specification of the Jumbo Payload option.

The specification of the TCP and UDP enhancements to support jumbograms previously appeared as RFC 2147, and RFC 2147 is obsoleted by this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The document joins two earlier pieces of work. The option itself used to be part of the IPv6 specification, and the changes to TCP and UDP used to be a separate RFC. This document is the single place that defines both, and it replaces that separate RFC.

sections.title: The Jumbo Payload Option Format
sections.content:
The Jumbo Payload option is carried in an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options header, immediately following the IPv6 header. It has an alignment requirement of 4n + 2.

The option has three fields. The Option Type is an 8-bit value of C2 in hexadecimal. The Opt Data Len is an 8-bit value of 4. The Jumbo Payload Length is a 32-bit unsigned integer giving the length of the IPv6 packet in octets, excluding the IPv6 header but including the Hop-by-Hop Options header and any other extension headers present. It must be greater than 65,535.
sections.plainLanguage: The option sits in a header that follows the IPv6 header, and it has three fields: a type byte, a length byte and a 32-bit number giving the true size of the packet. The size counts everything after the IPv6 header, including the extension headers.

sections.title: Using the Option and Reporting Errors
sections.content:
The Payload Length field in the IPv6 header must be set to zero in every packet that carries the Jumbo Payload option. If a node that understands the option receives a packet whose IPv6 header carries a Payload Length of zero and a Next Header value of zero, meaning that a Hop-by-Hop Options header follows, and whose link-layer framing indicates the presence of octets beyond the IPv6 header, the node must process the Hop-by-Hop Options header to determine the actual length of the payload from the Jumbo Payload option.

The Jumbo Payload option must not be used in a packet that carries a Fragment header. Higher-layer protocols that use the IPv6 Payload Length field to compute the Upper-Layer Packet Length field in the checksum pseudo-header must instead use the Jumbo Payload Length field, for packets that carry the option.

Nodes that understand the option are required to detect a number of possible format errors. Unless the erroneous packet was destined to a multicast address, they report the error by sending an ICMP Parameter Problem message (RFC 2463) to the packet's source. The RFC lists four errors, all with Code 0:

  • IPv6 Payload Length is 0, IPv6 Next Header is Hop-by-Hop Options and the Jumbo Payload option is not present. The Pointer is the high-order octet of the IPv6 Payload Length.
  • IPv6 Payload Length is not 0 and the Jumbo Payload option is present. The Pointer is the Option Type field of the option.
  • The option is present and the Jumbo Payload Length is below 65,536. The Pointer is the high-order octet of the Jumbo Payload Length.
  • The option is present and a Fragment header is present. The Pointer is the high-order octet of the Fragment header.

A node that does not understand the option is expected to respond to erroneously received jumbograms according to the IPv6 specification. For a Payload Length of 0 with a Hop-by-Hop Next Header, it uses Code 0 and points at the high-order octet of the Payload Length. For a Payload Length that is not 0 with the option present, it uses Code 2 and points at the Option Type field.
sections.plainLanguage: The normal size field in the IPv6 header is set to zero in every packet that uses the option, so a receiver knows to look at the option instead. If the two disagree, or if the option is missing when the size is zero, the receiver sends back an ICMP error naming the field at fault.

sections.title: UDP Jumbograms
sections.content:
The 16-bit Length field in the UDP header limits the total length of a UDP packet, header plus data, to no greater than 65,535 octets. This document relaxes that limit: UDP packets longer than 65,535 octets may be sent with the UDP Length field set to zero, and the receiver derives the actual length from the IPv6 payload length. Before this change, zero was not a legal value for the UDP Length field, because the UDP packet length includes the header and therefore has a minimum value of 8.

The requirements for sending are as follows. When sending a UDP packet, if and only if the length of the UDP header plus data is greater than 65,535, the sender sets the Length field to zero. The IPv6 packet carrying such a UDP packet necessarily includes a Jumbo Payload option, and the Jumbo Payload Length field is set to the actual length of the UDP header plus data, plus the length of all IPv6 extension headers present between the IPv6 header and the UDP header. For generating the UDP checksum, the actual length of the UDP header plus data is used, not zero, in the checksum pseudo-header.

The requirements for receiving are as follows. When receiving a UDP packet, if and only if the Length field is zero, the receiver calculates the actual length of the UDP header plus data from the IPv6 Jumbo Payload Length field minus the length of all extension headers present between the IPv6 header and the UDP header. In the unexpected case that the Length field is zero but no Jumbo Payload option is present, the receiver uses the Payload Length field of the IPv6 header in place of the Jumbo Payload Length field in that calculation. For verifying the received checksum, the calculated length is used, not zero.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP has a 16-bit length field of its own, so this RFC says a UDP packet longer than 65,535 bytes writes zero there instead. The receiver then works out the real length from the option and subtracts the extension headers in front of it. The checksum still uses the real length, not zero.

sections.title: TCP Jumbograms
sections.content:
There is no length field in the TCP header, so nothing limits the length of an individual TCP packet. Two values are still constrained to 16 bits. The MSS value negotiated at the beginning of the connection limits the largest TCP packet that can be sent, and the Urgent Pointer cannot reference data beyond 65,535 bytes.

For the MSS, when determining what value to send, if the MTU of the directly attached interface minus 60 is greater than or equal to 65,535, the sender sets the MSS value to 65,535. When an MSS value of 65,535 is received, it is treated as infinity: the actual MSS is determined by subtracting 60 from the value learned by performing Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1981) over the path to the TCP peer.

For the Urgent Pointer, the RFC notes that the problem could be fixed by adding a TCP Urgent Pointer Option, but since it is unlikely that applications using jumbograms will also use Urgent Pointers, a less intrusive change similar to the MSS change suffices. When a TCP packet is to be sent with an Urgent Pointer, the sender first calculates the offset from the Sequence Number to the Urgent Pointer. If the offset is less than 65,535, the Urgent field is filled in and normal processing continues. If the offset is greater than 65,535 and is greater than or equal to the length of the TCP data, the Urgent field is set to 65,535 and normal processing continues. Otherwise the packet must be split into two pieces: the first contains data up to, but not including, the data pointed to by the Urgent Pointer, and its Urgent field is set to 65,535 to indicate that the pointer is beyond the end of this packet; the second piece is then sent with the Urgent field set normally. The first piece does not have to include all of the data up to the Urgent Pointer, and can be shorter as long as it ends within 65,534 bytes of it, so that the offset in the second piece is less than 65,535 bytes.

On input, when a TCP packet is received with the URG bit set and an Urgent field of 65,535, the Urgent Pointer is calculated using an offset equal to the length of the TCP data, rather than the offset in the Urgent field. The RFC also notes that although the TCP window is only 16 bits, larger windows can be used through the TCP Window Scale option (RFC 1323).
sections.plainLanguage: TCP has no length field, but two of its values are limited to 16 bits. For the maximum segment size, the value 65,535 now means as large as the path allows. For the urgent pointer, the value 65,535 means the pointer lies at the end of the data, and the packet is split in two when the pointer is further away than that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the Jumbo Payload option and the TCP and UDP jumbograms do not introduce any known new security concerns. It says nothing further on the subject.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says the option and the TCP and UDP changes introduce no known new security concerns.

fields.name: Jumbo Payload Length
fields.desc: Packet length excluding the IPv6 header; it must be greater than 65,535.

viz.caption: THE FOUR FORMAT ERRORS, ALL WITH CODE 0

items.label: Option missing
items.desc: Payload Length is 0 and Next Header is Hop-by-Hop. Pointer: high-order octet of the Payload Length.

items.label: Option with a length
items.desc: Payload Length is not 0 and the option is present. Pointer: the Option Type field.

items.label: Length too small
items.desc: The Jumbo Payload Length is below 65,536. Pointer: high-order octet of that field.

items.label: Fragment header present
items.desc: The option and a Fragment header appear together. Pointer: high-order octet of the Fragment header.
